translation:
_Kabir char aadharme eku rahai, tab lagi ananya sant na hoy. Ananya taku pekhiye, tan dhan vidya kul khoy. ||2||_ (Kabir says: as long as even one of these four bases of mind remains, one cannot be called a true ananya — single-pointed, exclusive — saint. Recognize the ananya one as the one who gives up pride in body, wealth, learning, and lineage.)

Das Kabirji says that if even one of these four egoistic tendencies (mano-vrutti) remains, then until it is gone one cannot be called a saint of ananya conduct. Only one who abandons pride in body, wealth, and lineage can truly be called an ananya saint.

_Kabir kul tajyo to dhan rahyo, rahyo jaavan aadhar. Hari ichchha jaako nahi, sau kaiso ananya nirdhar. ||3||_ (Kabir says: even if one gives up pride of lineage, the pride of wealth remains, and the pride of youth remains as a support; one who has no surrender to Hari's will — how can such a person be called truly ananya?)

Das Kabirji says: even if someone has given up pride of lineage, an alluring attachment still lingers in him, along with the pride of youth, and if the disposition of devotion to God or of attaining God is absent, then how, indeed, can he be said with certainty to be an ananya devotee-saint?

_Kabir hari ichchhame jo chale, chhaand sakal karma dharma. Sahaj vrat jin grahi, soi ananya nishkarma. ||4||_ (Kabir says: one who walks according to Hari's will, giving up all ritual acts and duties, and who has taken up the vow of the natural, effortless state — that one alone is the true ananya, untouched by karma.)

Das Kabirji says: one who remains content with however God keeps him, abandoning every kind of ritual and ceremonial conduct, and who has taken up the discipline of remaining in the natural (sahaj) state — that one, untouched by karma, is called an ananya saint-devotee.

_Kabir ananya taku pekhiye, je sabhi chhaande aas. Hari charane laaga rahai, jaaka sahaj shoonyame vaas. ||5||_ (Kabir says: recognize as ananya the one who gives up every hope and expectation, who remains ever attached to Hari's feet, and whose natural state dwells fixed in the void.)

Das Kabirji says: one who gives up every hope and craving should be understood as an ananya saint-devotee — one who remains always joined in surrender at the feet of Hari, and whose natural state abides steadily fixed in the state of emptiness (shunya).

_Kabir saat paanch sangi ho rahai, kathe ananyako desh. Rahani karani aave nahi, pakha pakhi updesh. ||6||_ (Kabir says: those who gather in small groups of five or seven and speak of the way of the ananya devotees, yet do not let any partisan bias enter their conduct and way of living.)

Das Kabirji says: those who come together in small groups of five and seven and discuss the ideals of ananya devotees, and who do not let any kind of sectarian bias or partisan dispute enter into their conduct and manner of life — such are these devotees.

_Kabir rahani karani naha vikat hai, adhar jaaki aas. Paau palakka sangrah kare nahi, soi ananya nij daas. ||7||_ (Kabir says: this way of conduct and living according to the rule of ananya-ness is very hard — one whose hopes rest on nothing, who hoards nothing even for the span of a quarter of an eyeblink, that one alone is the Lord's own ananya devotee.)

Das Kabirji says: living according to the principles of ananya conduct is extremely difficult — it belongs to one who holds no expectations at all within, and who does not gather or store even the smallest thing, even for the time of a quarter of an eyeblink; that one alone is called the intimate ananya devotee of God.

_Kabir nishkami nirmohita, eko na thaathe kaam. Taako ananya ham kahat hai, sohi hamara nij daas. ||8||_ (Kabir says: one who is free of desire and free of attachment, in whom not a single craving takes root — that one we call ananya; that one alone is truly our own devotee.)

Das Kabirji says: one who is without any kind of desire and without delusion or attachment, in whom not a single craving arises — him we call ananya; he alone is our own intimate devotee.

_Kabir karma dharma sabku tajai, tajai kul vahaivar. Khaanpaan aan sab tajai, tajai tan dhan vidya aadhar. ||9||_ (Kabir says: he gives up all ritual actions and duties, gives up the customs and dealings of lineage, gives up all eating and drinking with those of another persuasion, and gives up reliance on body, wealth, and learning.)

Das Kabirji says: he gives up ritual observances and religious duties of every kind, gives up the customary conduct and dealings of his lineage, gives up all eating and drinking together with other worshippers of a different persuasion, and gives up placing reliance on the pride of body, wealth, and learning.

_Kabir tanmad dhanmad gyanmad, vidyamad unmad. Aite mad jab dil mile, tab soone naad anahad. ||11||_ (Kabir says: when the pride of body, the pride of wealth, the pride of knowledge, the pride of learning, and the pride of self all dissolve away from the heart, then the unstruck sound, the anahad naad, is heard.)

Das Kabirji says: when the pride of the body, the pride of wealth, the pride of worldly knowledge, and the pride of learning and of the self all merge and dissolve within the heart, then one experiences the divine sound — the direct experience of God's presence.

At Bapu Vrindavan's manuscript folio, book no. 9, at the end, on page 142, in describing the marks (lakshan) of the Vaishnav, thirty are listed: 1) the company of saints (satsang), 2) Hari's bhajan (devotional singing), 3) devotion to Hari (Hari bhakti), 4) loving feeling (bhav), 5) faith (shraddha), 6) humility (dinta), 7) modesty (vinay), 8) the disposition of a servant (das-bhav), 9) discernment (vivek), 10) reflection (vichar), 11) forgiveness (kshama), 12) contentment (santosh), 13) detachment (vairagya), 14) trust (vishwas), 15) compassion (karuna), 16) right understanding (sumati), 17) mercy (daya), 18) modesty at wrongdoing (lajja), [item 19 is missing from the source], 20) non-duality (abhed), 21) self-reflection (atma-vichar), 22) helping others (par-upkar), 23) restraint of ego (aham-sanyam), 24) the disposition of silence (mauna-bhav), 25) constant bliss (sada anand), 26) detachment from worldly concern (udasi), 27) knowing the body to be transient (kshanabhangur), 28) abstaining from food (printed "niraarapan", for niraahaarpan) and eating sparingly (alpa ahar), 29) gravity of temperament (gambhirta), and 30) freedom from egotism (aham-bhav rahit).

Thus, ritual-free (karmakand-rahit) Vaishnav devotion is the art of the swan (hansa-kala) — devotion practiced by discerningly separating the pure from the mixed, as a swan separates milk from water. It was for this reason that Vaishnav Jivandasji declared, speaking of the Lord of the Kali Yuga, that Ram-Krishna is the Lord of the Kali Yuga, and that the dharma of the Kali Yuga is ananya bhakti (single-minded, exclusive devotion). This samagam (holy discourse) took place at Shahapar. On the way back, whichever devotee-souls of matching disposition came at that time to meet Vaishnav Jivandasji, he revealed that same dharma to them — that is, he gave them the experience of that dharma according to their own feeling — and they became fulfilled.

Dada Jasvantji Weeps

Jasvantji wept — for whoever separates a devotee of Vishnu from his devotion must suffer hell.

The date — the samvat, month, and day — on which the episode of Dada Jasvantji occurred has been recorded; likewise, in another chapter, the occasion of when Haribhai came from Aritha to Shahapar has also been recorded with its samvat and date. Of the two, the Shahapar episode occurred first, and the Dada Jasvantji episode occurred afterward. But the earnest and discerning devotees who transcribed the samagam preserved this sequence, placing the Shahapar episode first and the Dada Jasvantji episode after it. We, however, have made no alteration in transcribing it, even where the original samagam may itself contain some discrepancy; therefore we present the Dada Jasvantji episode here exactly as it stands in the original.

This episode of Dada Jasvantji, as presented in the samagam, is very difficult to understand. This event, which occurred on the 13th day of the dark half of Bhadarva in Samvat 1707, has been narrated together with its precise date. On this day such anguish arose within Dada Jasvantji that his soul cried out in pain — hence it is said that Dada Jasvantji wept. Seeing him in this state of anguish, his daughter Janakibai asked him why he was so distressed. Explaining the cause of his anguish, Dada Jasvantji said:

"If some person, on account of the influence of an exclusive Vishnu devotee (Vishnu bhakti — devotion to Vishnu) such as us, causes another to fall, through association with him, onto the wrong path of ritual action (karma-marg), and that person then becomes engaged in the worship of Anadev (aan-dev — worship of 'another,' a different deity, as opposed to single-pointed, ananya devotion), then his soul will not be received into the community of ananya devotees — his soul will not be accepted as an ananya devotee within that community. But whoever tries to stop such a person from proceeding by the path of karma toward the worship of Anadev — whatever suffering of hell that other person would have had to bear, that very suffering will instead fall upon the one who tried to stop him. For this reason, it cannot be borne to watch it happen, and yet it cannot be stopped by watching it happen either — this is the painful dilemma that arises for any person who feels emotional concern for another.

An example given of this is the sage Sandipani, who asked Lord Krishna for his dead son back. For this reason, if a father and son, mother and daughter, father and son, or any siblings among themselves — brother and sister, or brother and brother — or father and daughter, being emotionally attached relatives, insist with stubbornness (hath) that one another practice Vishnu bhakti in a particular way, and try to stop the other from a different form of worship, then that person must bear hell in the other's place — he must bear hell on the other's behalf — and even the Vishnu bhakti that he himself has performed will go to waste. Such is the difficult situation that can arise. To make this clearer, a further example is given.

A snake bit and ate something, and the creature died; the snake was then killed for it. In this event, whatever karma there is attaches to the snake, but does not attach to the one who killed the snake. This is how it has been presented in the samagam — but this riddle is a difficult one; to help understand it, the earnest seekers who transcribed the samagam have set down their own views below.

Episode 1

On the 13th day of the dark half of Bhadarva, Samvat 1709, at a certain hour, Dado Jasvantji wept so that he might not be separated from his Guru — that is, his heart could not contain its love, and so he wept. His daughter Janakibai then asked, "Dadaji, why are you weeping?" He replied: "I weep because a certain soul, through the merit of Vishnu bhakti, took human birth. He was bhadra — that is, blessed by nature. But, dazzled by the sight of some worldly act, he became caught up in greed for worldly things. That soul has no room left in which to fall (jiya) — that is, no room left for it to fall, through ananya devotion, into surrender to God. If it should go under the shelter of Anadev, it will not be allowed to remain in surrender to God, because it has, again and again, turned away from the path of Vishnu bhakti — it has already seen and turned toward Anadev's worship instead. That soul has gone to hell. That soul now has work to do in the darkness of hell. Seeing this, I was moved to weep — because I am anxious about how I myself am to attain liberation, and it is out of the fear of being separated from my Guru that I weep — O Bhagavan!"

Episode 2

Sandipani's son had gone to hell. When the Lord became pleased with the sage, He established that son in Vaikuntha. At that time, Sandipani, out of his own longing, had the son called back to the mortal world. It is for this reason that, in the matter of Vishnu bhakti, Sandipani is said to have taken our own soul as the Lord's own, delivering it and rescuing it from the suffering of worldly existence. Therefore, if a wife and husband, mother and son, father and son, sister and brother, or any person among themselves, is practicing Vishnu bhakti, and someone causes it to be disrupted through stubbornness, superstition, or obstruction, then that person will suffer hell in the other's place, and — because he has obstructed that devotion — he himself will become disqualified and fall from grace. If he stubbornly restrains or obstructs another being from his devotion, misfortune will befall him. Moreover, however much disruption he causes, that other person will nonetheless go on practicing Vishnu bhakti and will, together with his whole family line, be sanctified — but the Vishnu bhakti of the one who caused the disruption will come to nothing, and he alone will suffer hell. Thus that being is affected in two ways. This is confirmed and upheld by scripture. If a snake bites someone, and before he dies he in his stubbornness kills the snake, the fruit of that killing attaches to the snake — for a snake never bites a person without provocation, or without some enmity carried over from a former life; yet because he stubbornly killed the serpent, the fault of that act will instead fall upon him as its fruit. In the same way, when a person practicing Vishnu bhakti, through the workings of karma, encounters happiness and sorrow, and becomes distraught and, through his own stubbornness, disrupts anyone's devotional practice — then, even though he himself continues practicing Vishnu bhakti, whatever ritual acts he performs will come to nothing. Therefore, whenever any person is engaged in the worship of God, one should remain accommodating toward him, and must never act against him in a way that disrupts his devotional practice.

There, the testimony of the Padma Purana — the same story is told at greater length in the Bhagavata, in the passage where the sage Kapilacharya instructs his mother; there the story is given in fuller detail. There, in the testimony of the Sahasranama, Mahadev spoke to Shri Vasudev the following corresponding verse —

_Brahmahatyaastoyapaapam shaamyodapi kathanchan, na punaatyasta krishnancha kalpakotishatairapi. ||64||_ (The sin of killing a Brahmin may perhaps, in some manner, be atoned for; but one who does not take the name of Krishna is not purified even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.)

Commentary: Shri Mahadevji said, "O Maharaj, no one is able to fully know the extent of your Vishnu bhakti. Although the scriptures hold that debt, enmity, and sin — these three — are never, at any time, released for anyone, so that not even the Supreme Lord can wipe them out by taking on, as it were, the office of a ferryman on the ship that carries one across — yet if such sins as the killing of a Brahmin and others are committed unknowingly, through some circumstance of karma, by an unrighteous person, that person can free himself by circumambulating the whole earth in pilgrimage, by journeying to all the sacred places (tirthas) of the universe, and by performing austerities while chanting the name of Ram. But whoever disrupts a devotee in whom the qualities of Shri Vasudev are being glorified — even if that person performs austerities for as many crores upon crores of ages as he wishes, he is never delivered. A person who obstructs a devotee of Shri Hari, or obstructs devotion to Shri Hari, falls into the Shaurava hell, and there suffers the very greatest torments for as long as the sun and moon shine, remaining undelivered through many kalpas." This is described in the Bhagavata and in the Padma Purana.

There, Kabirji's sakhi (couplet) —

_Kabir harika bhagatimaan, je kathaa chalaave aur. Taa aparaadhi jeevaka, teen lok nahi ger. ||1||_ (Kabir says: whoever spreads unworthy talk regarding devotion to the Lord — that sinful soul finds no resting place in any of the three worlds.)

Das Kabirji says: whoever, in the matter of devotion to God, sets in motion some unfit or unworthy discourse — that sinning soul finds no place to dwell anywhere in the three worlds.

I now set down my own view, corresponding to the episode of "Dada Jasvantji Wept" as described in the samagam.

Seeing Dada Jasvantji weeping, his daughter Janaki asked the reason for his tears. Dada explained that if a person practicing Vishnu bhakti were falling into the worship of Anadev, and someone stopped him from doing so, then the one who stopped him would have to suffer hell in that other person's place. Thus, either way, a difficult situation arises for the Vishnu devotee. As an example — Sandipani asked Krishna for his dead son back. Likewise, because of relationships such as father and son, brother and brother, or wife and husband, if we create obstruction or act with stubbornness, we must bear hell on the other's behalf. If a snake has eaten a frog, the one who then kills that snake does not incur the sin of killing the frog — that sin belongs to the snake; and if a snake bites someone who then dies, the one who kills the snake does not incur the sin of having killed that person — that too belongs to the snake. For this reason, the account of Sage Kapil in the Bhagavata should be understood. Kapil's father, the sage Kardam, was a son of Brahma. When Brahma directed his son to assist him in the work of creating the universe, Kardam performed austerities for ten thousand years, pleased the Lord, and asked for the boon, "Give me a wife." At this, tears came to the Lord's eyes, and from them arose the lake called Bindu Sarovar, which exists today in Siddhpur.

Let me set out my own view regarding Siddhpur. The meaning of "Siddhpur" is this: the place where siddhi (spiritual attainment) is reached — that "city" (pur) should be understood as the body. Without a body, no work can be accomplished, nor can siddhi be attained; yet even having obtained a body, if one falls into craving for siddhi (supernatural powers) and riddhi (worldly prosperity) — that is, if the body given by God's grace as a blessing is used in pursuit of siddhi or of maya — then, on seeing this, tears come to God's eyes; and although that tear is but a single drop, it becomes as vast as a lake. Because you hold expectation for wife, son, and the like, the Lord has had to "come" — to respond to that longing — and a son is produced from just a single drop, yet the family that results grows as broad as a lake. Kabirji, in the following section, has said —

_Ek boondke khaali gai, rona sab sansaar. Anek boond khaali gai, tinke kaun vichaar. ||15||_ (Kabir says: for the loss of a single drop the whole world weeps; but countless drops have gone to waste, and no one gives that any thought.)

Das Kabirji says: great effort is made for the sake of a single body formed from one drop, but no one gives any thought to the many bodies, formed from countless other drops, that have gone to waste without devotional practice.

You weep at the death of a person born from a single drop, but you do not consider that many other bodies, born from countless drops, have likewise gone to waste without devotional practice. In truth, the world itself is produced only from the drop that enters a mother's womb. Any child playing in a mother's lap is itself a form of God — one should not think it was born for no reason. There are as many bodies as there are grains of stone, and into one such body falls a teardrop of God, and thus a son is obtained; this drop is received by the mother, which is why special weight is given to maternal faith (matru-shraddha) in that connection. But ananya devotees have no need to cultivate faith centered on mother or father in this worldly sense — we are not meant to fall again and again into birth from a mother's or father's womb. So when the question of stubbornness arises, it should be pointed out that if we become bound up in ritual action out of regard for worldly relationships — father and son, brother and brother, brother and sister, mother and son, and so on — that too is itself a form of stubbornness, and it touches us not in one way but in many ways. This stubbornness comes in an extremely subtle form, so that we remain wholly unaware of it.

Kabirji, in the following section, said: for one drop the whole world weeps; you offer faith to one mother or one father, yet so many other drops have gone to waste, and you cannot offer faith to so many generations. Moreover, you show favoritism, you take sides — and so Kabir said:

_Kabir harijan nahi, bahu kutumbko bhaar. Gadhdha hokar otare, bhaanda bhare kumbhaar._ (Kabir says: one who is not a devotee of Hari carries the heavy burden of a large household; he takes birth as a donkey, and the potter loads pots and vessels upon his back.)

Das Kabirji says: those who are not devotees of Hari carry upon their heads a very heavy burden of family and household. Because of this, they take birth as a donkey, and the potter loads the burden of vessels upon their back and makes them labor. Through this potter-like Brahma, one must bear, across the eighty-four lakh species, the burden of the body — like a vessel — of birth, again and again.

The potter is Prajapati — he is Brahma, and he is regarded as the presiding deity of Pitrulok, the realm of the ancestors. By performing deeds aimed at worldly attainment, one bears, many times over, the burden of the body of birth across the eighty-four lakh species. A devotee of Hari, however, does not carry the burden of being born into so many kinds of families. In this way, people generally remain inattentive toward karma that attaches to them in subtle ways; devotees of Hari, by contrast, remain ever vigilant.

Although Lord Kapil was himself, in essence, greater than his own father, he did not come forward on his own to instruct Sage Kardam. Kardam was spending the power of his austerities in pleasures with his wife, Devahuti, and Kapil made no attempt to stop him. Only when Kardam came to realize, "This one, in the form of my son, is God," and sought knowledge from him, did the Lord give his teaching. In the same way, when the mother too came to understand, "This one, in the form of my son, is God," he gave her the teaching of Sankhya philosophy. So the purpose of presenting this episode from the Bhagavata within Jivanji Maharaj's samagam is this: even though one may oneself be God, one must never — on the basis of any relationship, whether as father, mother, son, or otherwise — act with even the slightest stubbornness to restrain or stop another; nor should one do so. Even though Arjun was as close as a friend, Krishna — though called Jagadguru, the teacher of the universe — became his instructor, but did not become his guru in the sense of one who imposes authority.

This subject is a very subtle one. Just as a person's inner vital essence (sattva) diminishes when he begets a son, this same principle applies to any undertaking whatsoever. Indeed, even in giving an order to a servant, your merit (punya) is diminished, even though you may be paying him a wage. Thus, with each and every word we utter, the consciousness (chaitanya) residing within us is set into motion and expended. This is why sages strive, through silence, to conserve themselves. A guru who gives teaching transmits into his disciple a portion of the power dwelling within himself; thereby that guru's power comes to reside within the disciple. This transmission is called "paat" — a falling, or passing over. Just as a man passes semen into a woman, so too do we, in various ways, pass on our own inner essence. When we try to direct our son, our wife, or society in any particular direction, our own inner power is expended in the effort. This is why we cannot easily grasp so profound a subject; Jivanji has explained it very concisely. Even in telling someone, "Open the door," we lose some of our own vital force. A difficult problem arises on both sides — whether to restrain someone or not to restrain them — so the objection that the matter remains unresolved is not acceptable. Even where one does good, the possibility of wrongdoing does not disappear; the rule that good done by a person results in good for that person does not always hold true. So then — should one do good, or not?

_Duniya sab dhokhe muvaayaan, kare kutumbki kaan. Jab kul kiska laajasi, jab le dharaa masaan._ (Kabir says: the whole world dies deceived, caught up in concern for family honor; but when the body is carried to the cremation ground, whose lineage will then feel shame?)

Das Kabirji says: in the delusion of worldly pleasures and the like, people go about consumed with concern for the honor and reputation of family; but when the body is carried to the cremation ground, where then will the family's honor remain? The body is transient; pride taken in it is false.

Once the cremation ground is reached, whose lineage will feel shame — is there anything left to protect? Therefore, one should not, deceived by delusion, fall into concern for family reputation. At the time of death, it is your devotion that will be shamed if found lacking; therefore, having become a devotee, one should practice devotion by breaking free of concern for worldly reputation, family, and honor.

Stubbornness in the matter of Vishnu bhakti can be shown in many forms. For instance: (1) Once, the wedding procession of the world-guru Shankaracharya was passing through Dwarka on an elephant. He had the elephant halted on the way, got down, and, seeing a Brahmin bearing a Swaminarayan tilak on his forehead, tore off and took away his sacred thread, rebuking him harshly: "Shame and disgrace! Being a Brahmin, you wear a Vaishnavi tilak — Brahmins should apply only sacred ash." Even a powerful world-guru had to act in this way — and in this episode too, there is stubbornness. Whether for a Vishnu devotee or for a Shiva devotee, stubbornness is truly present; this creates a tangled situation even for religious authorities. Thus the presence of stubbornness persists in virtually every kind of conduct.

Whether someone smokes, gambles, drinks liquor, or performs any good or bad act — whether to stop him or not is itself a difficult question. (2) The consecration of the life-breath (pran-pratishtha) into an idol is likewise a form of stubbornness — an insistence on making God dwell within it. (3) Vows, petty religious disputes, sacred threads and charms, votive offerings, and the like are all forms of stubbornness. (4) Even the enjoyment of the pleasures created by God is enjoyed at the cost of one's own depleting merit (punya). If sin comes through stubbornness, then merit, too, has stubbornness as its cause. Whether we use water freely or use it sparingly, we shall still have to give an account of it to God — "How much of My water did you use? How much of My grain did you use?" — and so on. Just as a servant must give an account to his master, so too must we give our account.

_Kasugandha vanitaa vastram, geetam taambool bhojanam. Bhooshanam vaahanam cheti, bhogashatakamudeeriyatam._ (Fine fragrance, a woman's company, clothing, singing, playing music, chewing betel leaf, eating food, ornaments, and conveyance — these are the eight kinds of enjoyment; indulging in them causes the depletion of merit.)

This chapter concerns the event known as "Dada Jasvantji Wept," which took place in his life on the 13th day of the dark half of Bhadarva, Samvat 1709. As to who Dada Jasvantji was — the explanation is found by reflecting on the words used in the description given in verse 5 of the Bhaktamal of Jivanji Maharaj, composed by Haridas Nadiyada; considering those words clarifies who Dada Jasvantji was. It is recorded there, in verse 5. There are two variant readings of this verse — one as found in the guru lineage (guru-pranalika) recorded within the Bhaktamal in the samagam, and another as found in the lineage recorded in Handwritten Manuscript No. 44-Jha, page 31. The variant reading between the two is as follows:

Samagam, Verse 5 —

_Dvaadas jan apudeshmaan, sukhdaataa jethaa bhayaa. Taake shikh gopaalajee, jan joovan updesh diyaa._

According to this, among Ramanand's twelve disciples, the foremost, who gave the joy and bliss of loving devotion (prem-bhakti), was Kabirji. In his lineage came Gnaniji; his disciple was Dada Sukhji; and his disciple was Gopaldasji, who gave instruction to Jivandasji.

Handwritten Manuscript 44, Verse 1 —

_Dvaarakaadaas updeshmen, sukhdaataa jaag bhayaa. Taake shikh gopaalajee, jan jeevanku updesh diyaa._

According to this, Gnaniji's rajguru (royal preceptor) was Khojiji-Dwarakadas. Gnaniji's chief disciple, who gave the joy of loving devotion, was Dada Sukhji (Jasvantji); his disciple was Gopadasji, who gave instruction to Jivandasji.

Thus, according to what is stated in this text, in interpreting "Sukhdata Jetha," the view that Sukhdata Jetha refers to Dada Jasvant was put forward by Nazar Damodardas Purushottam, following the advice and opinion of the Revered Yadunath Maharaj; his account of this is as follows (reference: Jagdish No. 1465, page 206):

It appears that Jasvantji, the disciple of Gnaniji, must have had "Dado Sakhji" as another name. This seems evident because the name Jasvantji appears in the earlier verse, while in the guru lineage recorded in the samagam, we find "Dado Sakhji, of Pipavans, resident of Shukla Tirth." Weighing all this together — if each of these names belonged to a separate person, a great many years would need to have passed between them, which is not plausible; hence it appears that all these names belong to one and the same person. This is the view expressed by Puniyad Swami Yadunathji, and on reflection it seems the same to me as well. Between Jivanji Maharaj and Gnaniji Maharaj only two generations passed — Gopaldas and Dado Sukhji — this is a matter of common, well-known record; therefore, Dado Sakhji, Dado Jasvant, and the person addressed as Sukhdata Jetha are one and the same.

My own view is likewise that, in Jivanji's guru lineage, the guru of Gopaldas is called Dada Sukhji, and in this chapter it is said that "Dada Jasvantji wept." Thus the title "Dada" occurs in both cases, and Revered Yadunathji's view — that these two are one and the same — is, in my judgment, correct.

Thus, having noted the date on which this Dada-guru of Jivanji Maharaj experienced this event, mention has been made here of his devotion. This shows the depth of Jasvantji's feeling, and in support of it, a sakhi of Kabirji has also been given, declaring that whoever conducts himself wrongly in matters of devotion to Hari is as much at fault as one who acts with stubbornness. Kabir has said —

_Kabir khanchaataani mat karau, utaro bhav jal paar. Niranjan niraakaar au kahiye, sau raavan kumbhakarn sanharanaar._ (Kabir says: do not engage in excessive insistence and stubbornness; practice devotion, and you will cross the ocean of worldly existence. The one we call the formless, attributeless Brahman is that same Ram who destroyed Ravana and Kumbhakarna.)

Das Kabirji says: O brother, do not engage in excessive insistence and stubbornness — practice devotion to Ram, and you will cross the ocean of worldly existence. The one whom we call the formless, attributeless (nirgun-nirakar) Brahman is that same Ram who destroyed Ravana and Kumbhakarna.

_Kabir harikee bhakti bin, je kije aparaadh. Kahvo sunvo bolvo, sab karvo aparaadh._ (Kabir says: whatever worship you perform apart from devotion to Hari — speaking of it, hearing it, or discussing it — all of it is sinful.)

Das Kabirji says: whatever other worship one performs apart from devotion to God — speaking of it, listening to it, or discussing it — all of this is sinful and faulty.

The date of the episode "Dada Jasvantji Wept" is the 13th day of the dark half of Bhadarva, in the year Samvat 1709; the scribe adds the note "lakhu e lakhu daahathaa panar vityaa" — written thus, fifteen days having passed from that date. After this chapter, the samagam records, in several places, the dates on which certain further episodes occurred. The next episode given in the samagam took place fifteen days after Jasvantji wept.
